name: Horn effect
statement: One unfavourable impression of a person is said to drag down judgements of everything else about them, the negative counterpart of the halo effect.
meaning: The claim borrows its structure from the halo effect and reverses the sign. Halo says a good impression bleeds into unrelated ratings. Horn says a bad one does the same, and management writing usually adds that it does so harder. That last part is a separate claim and it has to be shown rather than assumed. An effect can run in both directions and still be symmetrical, in which case the second name is decoration. The halo entry, number 23, carries Thorndike's original rating data and the argument about what halo error is. The pooled record on beauty and judgement sits at entry 505. This entry is about whether the negative half stands on anything of its own.

origin.note: Thorndike's "A constant error in psychological ratings" describes the error in both directions. He writes that raters showed a tendency to think of the person in general as rather good or rather inferior and to colour the judgements of the qualities by this general feeling. He never names a negative version. The words horn, horns and negative halo appear nowhere in the paper, which was searched on its own text rather than on a summary of it. Where the name itself came from could not be established.

evidence: One research programme tests the claim under the name. Mattavelli, Brambilla, Koch and Dono ran four experiments on Prolific, 1,418 valid respondents in total. Experiment 1 was not preregistered and the other three were. In the first, 228 of 302 recruits generated their own moral and able behaviours, then rated them on the opposite dimension. Spread was larger from immoral behaviours to inability than from unable behaviours to immorality, t(226) = -4.36, p < .001, d = 0.58. The matching contrast for positive behaviours was flat, t(226) = 0.12, p = .906, d = 0.02. Experiments 2a and 2b, pooled to 487 valid respondents, moved the judgement from acts to people. Participants saw four male faces from the Chicago Face Database, each paired with one negative behaviour, and the asymmetry held, F(1, 485) = 5.54, p = .019, eta squared 0.008. The last experiment, which the paper numbers 3, kept 703 respondents of 806 and reproduced it at F(1, 699) = 68.12, p < .001, eta squared 0.065. Targets tied to an immoral act scored -1.51 on ability, while targets tied to an incompetent act sat at -0.55 on morality. Perceived threat mediated the gap, indirect effect -0.38, interval -0.56 to -0.23. The other line of evidence is the physical attractiveness stereotype, and it bears on the horn question through a design detail rather than through its pooled sizes, which are at entry 505. Langlois and five colleagues, having reviewed over 900 effect sizes, wrote that they could conclude only that attractive and unattractive people are judged, treated and behave differently. Almost every study had used two levels of attractiveness. Because they did not know whether either group differed from people of medium attractiveness, they could not tell whether attractiveness is an advantage, unattractiveness a disadvantage, or both. Griffin and Langlois used three levels. They built six matched sets of three female faces, which an independent sample of 61 undergraduates rated at means of 1.50, 2.39 and 3.41 on a five-point scale. Then 285 undergraduates, of 331 recruited, rated each face on sociability, altruism and intelligence. Attractiveness mattered, Wilks's lambda 0.34, F(6, 279) = 90.35, p < .001, eta squared 0.66. The shape of it is the finding. Unattractive faces were rated below medium faces on all three domains, while medium faces fell below attractive faces on sociability alone. A second experiment with 115 children of 120 tested, aged 7 to 9, gave the same pattern, Wilks's lambda 0.47, F(6, 109) = 20.12, p < .001, eta squared 0.53. The authors conclude that it is more often the case that unattractiveness is bad than that beauty is good, and read the asymmetry as negativity bias. Earnings belong to neither line, because a wage is not a rating. Hamermesh and Biddle used interviewer ratings of respondents' looks in three North American surveys. Plain people earn less than people of average looks, they report, who earn less than the good-looking. Their published article puts the penalty at 7 to 9 percent for the lowest 9 percent of looks, and the premium at 5 percent for the top 33 percent. It then says that the difference between penalty and premium is not significant, and that there is only weak evidence of asymmetry in how the labour market treats ugliness and beauty. That second sentence is the one this page has to carry.

replication.headline: Both papers repeat themselves, no independent laboratory has repeated either, and the only head-to-head test of horn against halo is the weakest experiment in its own paper.
replication.detail: Mattavelli and colleagues compared positive spread with negative spread in Experiment 1 alone. Generalisation was larger for positive behaviours, mean 3.04, than for negative ones, mean 2.38, F(1, 226) = 32.18, p < .001, eta squared 0.033. Their own discussion then warns that the asymmetry they cared about may be an artefact of the stimuli. Participants generated the behaviours themselves, and the moral ones came out more extreme than the ability ones. Positive behaviours were also rated more extreme than negative ones, 3.99 against 3.43. Experiments 2a, 2b and 3 dropped the positive condition and tested the negative half alone. So the valence comparison rests on one experiment that was not preregistered and that its authors treat as a starting point. What does repeat in their data sits inside the negative half. Immorality dragged down ability ratings more than incompetence dragged down morality ratings, three times over, each time under preregistration. Griffin and Langlois repeat their own result in children, and it points the other way on valence, since their stereotype loaded on its negative end. The two designs are not comparable. One attributes traits to faces, and the other tracks spread between two content dimensions of judgement.

study.cite: Mattavelli, S., Brambilla, M., Koch, A., & Dono, M. (2026). "If Immoral Then Unable": Asymmetric Generalizations in Social Judgment. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin. Published online, no volume or pages yet.

limits: Searches below were run on 21 September 2026. A Crossref bibliographic search for horn effect and horns effect returns nothing in psychology; the hits are dorsal horns, uterine horns, loudspeaker horns and brass instruments. The single record under the name is a two-page reference-work entry, Horns effect in the Encyclopedia of Human Resource Management. Its landing page refuses a plain request with HTTP 403 and serves normally to a browser user agent, so the obstacle is a bot check and not, as this page said in August, closed access. The bibliographic record, the page range and the entry's whole reference list are readable, and the text itself needs a subscription this audit does not have. That reference list cites performance-appraisal work rather than a founding study, and it names no Campbell and Knowlton. A PubMed title and abstract search on the same date returns eight records. Four of them concern impression formation, not two as this page said in August, and two use the name for the thing this entry is about. Paruzel-Czachura, Workman, El Toukhy and Chatterjee rated faces photographed before and after plastic surgery, and closed by calling the anomalous-is-bad pattern a reverse halo effect, that is, the horn effect. Burris, Kular and Knox tested what people assume about targets described as evil, and set the work beside the horns or negative halo effect. Both were read as PubMed abstracts only. Wiley and PhilArchive each returned HTTP 403 to this session, and Europe PMC records no open copy, so no figure from either paper is quoted here. Griffin and Langlois print no means or effect sizes for the individual contrasts. Those appear only in their figures, and the multivariate statistics quoted here are what the text carries. Their subject is what people infer from a face, not what happens to an appraisal form. The Hamermesh and Biddle numbers now come from the journal article, read as a scan of American Economic Review 84(5), pages 1174 to 1194. The 1993 working paper is not identical. It gives a 7 to 10 percent penalty for the lowest 10 percent of looks and a 5 percent premium for the top 30 percent, where the article gives 7 to 9 percent, the lowest 9 percent and the top 33 percent. The working-paper abstract says the effects are slightly larger for men than women; the article says effects for men are at least as great as for women. The 5 to 10 percent headline figure survives both. The same authors later re-tested the earnings question on the graduates of one law school, and that working-paper abstract reports no impact of beauty on earnings among 1980s graduates. Only the abstract was read. Mattavelli and colleagues use horn effect to mean generalisation from negative information, which is narrower than the workplace usage, and nothing here tests whether a single bad trait contaminates a whole appraisal form.
misreadings: The line repeated most often in management writing is that the horn effect is stronger than the halo effect. The only experiment that has put the two side by side found the reverse for overall spread, and its authors do not offer that as a result. They warn in the same discussion that their stimuli were self-generated and unevenly extreme, and they dropped the positive condition from every later experiment. Nobody has yet run the comparison well. The asymmetry Mattavelli and colleagues did find is a different thing. Within negative information, immorality spread to ability judgements more than the other way round. That is a claim about morality, not about valence, and quoting it as proof that bad news travels further misstates it. A second error attributes the term to Thorndike. His 1920 paper describes raters colouring every quality with a general impression of a person as rather good or rather inferior, which covers the negative direction, but he coined halo and nothing else. Sources online date the name to a 1956 training manual by Campbell and Knowlton. No such work was found in Crossref or Open Library on 21 September 2026, the Wikipedia article on the horn effect does not make the claim, and it appears to originate in an automatically generated encyclopedia page. A third error is the one this page used to make itself. Hamermesh and Biddle get quoted as showing that ugliness costs more than beauty pays. Their abstract does say the plainness penalty is slightly larger than the beauty premium. Their results section says the difference is not significant and the evidence of asymmetry weak, and their footnote adds that any asymmetry may reflect how beauty was rated rather than how the market treats it. A wage recorded in a survey is not a rating made in an experiment, and a regression on observational data is not a repeat of one. Griffin and Langlois are cited loosely in the other direction. Their unattractive faces lost ground against the middle of the scale on all three domains. Nobody was downgraded on a trait they had been rated highly on.

sources.text: Thorndike, E. L. (1920). A constant error in psychological ratings. Journal of Applied Psychology, 4(1), 25-29. Read in full from a scan hosted by MIT, and searched on whole words for horn, horns and negative halo, none of which occur.

Griffin, A. M., & Langlois, J. H. (2006). Stereotype directionality and attractiveness stereotyping: Is beauty good or is ugly bad? Social Cognition, 24(2), 187-206. Read in full at PubMed Central, PMC1447532. The source for the three-level design, the analysed sample sizes of 285 and 115, and every statistic attributed to it.

Langlois, J. H., Kalakanis, L., Rubenstein, A. J., Larson, A., Hallam, M., & Smoot, M. (2000). Maxims or myths of beauty? A meta-analytic and theoretical review. Psychological Bulletin, 126(3), 390-423. Read in full. Cited here only for the statement that two-level designs cannot separate advantage from disadvantage; its pooled effects are quoted at entry 505.

Mattavelli, S., Brambilla, M., Koch, A., & Dono, M. (2026). "If Immoral Then Unable": Asymmetric Generalizations in Social Judgment. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin. Read in full from the typeset copy on the second author's website; data and preregistrations at https://osf.io/rfa76/. Published online, with no volume or page numbers yet.

Hamermesh, D. S., & Biddle, J. E. (1994). Beauty and the labor market. American Economic Review, 84(5), 1174-1194. Read as a page scan of the whole article. The source for the 7 to 9 percent penalty, the 5 percent premium, and the authors' statement that the difference between them is not significant. No DOI is registered for this article.
Hamermesh, D. S., & Biddle, J. E. (1993). Beauty and the labor market. NBER Working Paper 4518. Read in full. Held for comparison with the journal version, whose figures differ.

Rowley, C., Ramasamy, N., & Cox, A. (2023). Horns effect. In Encyclopedia of Human Resource Management, pages 172-173. Edward Elgar. The only reference-work record Crossref returns under the name. The landing page returns HTTP 403 to a plain request and loads for a browser user agent, giving the record and the entry's reference list; the text needs a subscription and was not read.

Paruzel-Czachura, M., Workman, C. I., El Toukhy, N., & Chatterjee, A. (2024). First impressions: Do faces with scars and palsies influence warmth, competence and humanization? British Journal of Psychology, 115(4), 706-722. Named here because its abstract calls the pattern a reverse halo effect, that is, the horn effect. Only the PubMed abstract was read; Wiley and PhilArchive returned HTTP 403 on 21 September 2026 and Europe PMC records no open copy.

Burris, C. T., Kular, S. I., & Knox, C. (2026). Damned if they do, damned if they don't: Lay assumptions about "evil" individuals' everyday behaviours. International Journal of Psychology, 61(1), e70158. Named here because its abstract places the work beside the horns or negative halo effect. Only the PubMed abstract was read.

Biddle, J. E., & Hamermesh, D. S. (1995). Beauty, productivity and discrimination: Lawyers' looks and lucre. NBER Working Paper 5366. The same authors re-testing the earnings question on one law school's graduates. Only the abstract page was read, which reports no impact of beauty on earnings among 1980s graduates.
